Fig1: Fig. 1 How tested genes enter the disease model through the normalization denominator. a, The whole-library route carries test counts into the effective denominator, the normalized marker inputs, and hence the composition-adjusted coefficient. The cross marks the link blocked by marker restriction under the same test-only change. Marker counts, outcomes, samples and tested genes stay fixed. b, Analytic sensitivity of the log-transformed marker input to the log denominator. c, Finite changes at fixed marker counts for denominator increases of 10%, 25% and 50%. Curves follow Eq. (1)
Fig2: Fig. 2 Inferential changes under paired normalization controls. a, FDR with direct effects of 0.5 in 20 of 100 test genes. b, Coverage for the 80 unaffected genes. c, Proportion RMSE. Each condition used 80 mixtures of 200 nuclei and 200 repetitions per target donor. L-in and S-in denote six internal LIBD and SEA-AD targets; L-ext and S-ext denote the same 15 GSE174367 targets under the respective reference. Points are donor-equal means; whiskers are 95% Monte Carlo intervals conditional on donor banks. Dotted lines mark 5% FDR and 95% coverage. All planned tests were available
Fig3: Fig. 3 Pseudocount scale changes both denominator sensitivity and calibration. Panels a–d show L-in, S-in, L-ext and S-ext. Curves compare observed and paired fixed denominators at five pseudocount-to-scale ratios, with direct effects of 0.5 in 20 test genes. Points are donor-equal FDR estimates and whiskers are 95% Monte Carlo intervals. The response, sampled nuclei and test family are fixed within each paired comparison. The dotted line marks 5%. Donor banks and repetition counts follow Fig. 2
Fig4: Fig. 4 Relative improvement and absolute FDR across the marker-dose grid. a, MRN-minus-TMM global-null FDR (percentage points). b, Absolute MRN global-null FDR (%). The outlined cells in a and b show the same SEA-AD external setting at 20% markers and amplitude 1.0. c, MRN-minus-TMM power with 20 direct effects of 0.5. Blocks retain the planned marker fractions; columns within a block show increasing amplitude. Printed values mark the highest amplitude in each block. Colors represent all donor-equal estimates. Open circles in b mark absolute FDR estimates above 5%; the outlines identify the paired design contrast. Neither marking is a significance test. Each donor contributed 200 paired repetitions of 80 mixtures. Table S4 gives every estimate and its Monte Carlo interval for paired differences; marker quotas are in Online Resource 1, Section S4
Fig5: Fig. 5 Common-support allocation separates zero filling from persistent marker sensitivity. Panels a–d show L-in, S-in, L-ext and S-ext. Lines connect donor-equal global-null FDR under zero-allowing and positive-only allocation for predefined, reference-feature-matched and random subsets. Circles show TMM and squares show MRN; open symbols denote zero-allowing allocation and filled symbols denote positive-only allocation. Matched and random entries each average three fixed subsets within donor. Both support rules and all perturbed subsets share the same reduced sample-by-class count budget. Each unit used 50 repetitions; six internal or 15 external target donors contributed. The dotted line marks 5% FDR
Fig6: Fig. 6 Similar proportion errors accompany different global-null FDRs under marker restriction. a,b, Proportion RMSE and FDR for the LIBD reference and 15 external GSE174367 target donors, with the predefined subset, all three random subsets and their equal-weight mean. Subset results were averaged within donor first. c–e, Internal LIBD, internal SEA-AD and external SEA-AD. Squares denote reference-feature-matched subsets; crosses are unperturbed controls. Perturbed subsets received the same sample-by-class count budgets on baseline-positive entries, with 50 repetitions per unit. Dotted lines mark 5% FDR
Fig7: Fig. 7 Marker restriction increases coefficient variation and reduces power in unperturbed mixtures. a,b, Power at effects 0.1, 0.25 and 0.5 in the internal LIBD and SEA-AD settings. Whiskers are 95% Monte Carlo intervals. c, Signed changes from TMM to MRN in composition-projection variance, noise-projection variance and twice their covariance, for 20 affected genes at effect 0.25 in internal SEA-AD mixtures. The endpoints give total coefficient-error variance. The percentage is the composition increment divided by the total variance increment. Components were calculated within gene over the same 200 repetitions and then averaged over genes and six target donors. d, Paired donor mean coefficients; larger symbols give donor-equal means. All fits used 80 mixtures and returned all planned tests
Fig8: Fig. 8 Clinical disease coefficients and discovery membership under TMM and MRN. a,b, Density of paired coefficients for the same 16,161 non-marker genes. Both references use the same coefficient limits and color scale for the number of genes per bin. The dashed line marks equality. Symbols identify genes significant only under TMM (triangles) or only under MRN (circles). c, Full-family discoveries shared by both fits or unique to one, with filled bars for LIBD and outlined bars for SEA-AD. Genes significant under neither fit are included in the density. d, Empirical cumulative distributions of gene-wise standard-error ratios. The sample set (218 Alzheimer disease and 70 control), age, sex, responses and tested genes were fixed. Table S10 gives discovery totals
Fig9: Fig. 9 Count share, effective denominator and clinical consequences of test-count perturbations. a, Change in the effective TMM denominator when the full tested family was decreased or increased in Alzheimer disease (AD) samples; points and whiskers are medians and interquartile ranges for AD and control samples. b, Signed change in each selected gene’s own disease coefficient, ordered by its baseline count share. Triangles encode the direction and fill identifies the reference. c,d, Percentage of the 16,161 genes crossing the full-family BH threshold of 0.05 under LIBD and SEA-AD. The input dose is 100[exp(t) − 1] for t = 0.01, 0.05 and 0.10. Complete exclusion, denominator-only normalization and MRN overlap at zero. Responses and the BH family were fixed. Crossings describe changes in significance status; clinical false discoveries were not observed. Tables S13 and S20 provide the numerical results
FigS1: Fig. S1 FDR and coverage with nonzero direct effects in the relative-count grid. a, MRN FDR. b, MRN coverage. c, MRN-minus-TMM coverage. Twenty test genes had direct effect 0.5. Shading gives the donor-equal means over 200 paired repetitions; numbers mark amplitude 1.0 in each marker-fraction block. Open circles in a mark FDR estimates above 5%. Settings and marker quotas follow Fig. 4
FigS2: Fig. S2 Common-support dose retention varies across settings and cell classes. a, Pooled percentage of requested counts retained in each setting, summed over 50 draws per target donor. b, Retention by marker class. Values are percentages of requested counts; classes follow the fixed marker assignments. Every subset and support rule receives the same retained sample-by-class budget. All 2,100 draws retain positive total budgets, although individual sample-by-class budgets may be zero
FigS3: Fig. S3 Denominator-only and full marker-restricted normalization have similar inferential performance. Panels show MRN-minus-denominator-only differences in global-null FDR, power with 20 direct effects of 0.25 and proportion RMSE under positive-only common-support allocation. Points are donor-equal contrasts for predefined subsets or the within-donor means of three matched or random subsets. Each unit used 50 paired repetitions. No confidence interval is represented by these descriptive points
FigS4: Fig. S4 Clinical disease alignment with the nuisance space. a, Disease-exposure R² against the nuisance space containing age, sex and estimated composition. b, Residualized-exposure sum of squares. Points compare the five composition-input rules under LIBD and SEA-AD references. All ten models have six composition contrasts and 16,161 available genes. Samples and disease labels are fixed
FigS5: Fig. S5 Donor-level marker associations in clinical single-nucleus data. Panels show owner-class log2 fold-change point estimates for the LIBD and SEA-AD panels in GSE174367. Primary models adjusted for age, source-recorded sex and batch. Each point is a testable marker; horizontal jitter separates points within class. Bars give class medians and dotted lines mark ±log2(1.5). No marker passed the planned-family BH threshold of 0.05. The candidate cohort contained 18 donors; class-specific eligibility is given in Online Resource 1, Section S7
FigS6: Fig. S6 Actual nuisance-span reporting separates estimability from a fixed-rank rule. The same MEAD point predictions and injected outcomes enter a rule requiring six composition contrasts and an actual-span rule. Panels show test availability, conditional coverage, delivered coverage and FDR with 20 direct effects of 0.5. Points give donor-equal means and whiskers give 95% Monte Carlo intervals over 200 repetitions per target. HC3 and leverage criteria are retained in both rules. Dotted lines mark 95% coverage or 5% FDR
FigS7: Fig. S7 Local derivative reliability and numerical invariance. a, Planned, finite and qualified simulation diagnostic records per method and outcome; counts are identical across the two outcomes. Qualified scores in all five invariant arms are zero after the 10⁻⁶ floor. TMM and factor-only exclusion have no qualified records. b,c, Clinical relative derivative disagreement for TMM and factor-only exclusion under LIBD and SEA-AD references, across four central-difference steps. The dotted line is the qualification threshold of 0.1. These checks assess approximation reliability rather than FDR control
FigS8: Fig. S8 Coefficient changes under fixed-response perturbations in four workflows. Panels a and b show global-null outcomes; c and d have 20 direct effects of 0.5. Panels a and c add test counts; b and d add marker counts. Points show donor-equal RMS coefficient changes, and bars show one conditional Monte Carlo standard error from 200 repetitions per unit and outcome. L and S denote LIBD and SEA-AD references; in and ext denote internal and GSE174367 targets. Panel scales differ (Table S16)
FigS9: Fig. S9 Paired changes in global-null FDR and power with 20 direct effects under tested-count and marker-count probes. Points are donor-equal changes from baseline in percentage points. Error bars are conditional 95% Monte Carlo intervals with references and target donors held fixed (Table S17)
FigS10: Fig. S10 Clinical coefficients, BH threshold crossings and fit availability in two brain cohorts. a–c, Fusiform-gyrus cohort. d–f, Prefrontal cohort. The first two panels in each row give paired changes from the same workflow at baseline. The third panel records availability separately for the LIBD and SEA-AD references. OK denotes an estimable comparison, M insufficient marker coverage and H a non-estimable HC3 fit. Unavailable comparisons have no plotted value; an estimable comparison with no change is plotted at zero. Markers distinguish tested-count from marker-count perturbations. Tables S18 and S19 give fit diagnostics and numerical contrasts
FigS11: Fig. S11 Marker restriction and error against tissue-block imaging measurements. Each point is MRN minus TMM donor-weighted mean absolute error in percentage points for one cell class and reference. Negative values indicate lower error under marker restriction. Technical libraries were averaged within a tissue block, losses were averaged within donor, and donors received equal weight. The paired transfer panels use reference-derived markers; the original clinical panels did not meet marker coverage in all classes. The 14 libraries correspond to seven blocks in five held-out donors; the two columns report support for each class. Table S21 gives the absolute errors and paired differences
